case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Double Jeopardy Clause permits Georgia to vacate an acquittal as “repugnant” (i.e., void) and retry the defendant for the same offense after a jury has returned an acquittal on that count alongside an inconsistent conviction on another count.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution, Fifth Amendment Double Jeopardy Clause (as incorporated against the States via the Fourteenth Amendment).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: McElrath argues that an acquittal—however inconsistent with another verdict—triggers absolute double jeopardy protection, so Georgia’s practice of labeling certain inconsistent verdict pairs “repugnant,” vacating the acquittal as void, and allowing retrial impermissibly nullifies the jury’s not-guilty verdict and exposes him to a second prosecution for the same offense. He contends “repugnant” verdicts are essentially just a subset of inconsistent verdicts, which under Supreme Court doctrine do not allow the State to upset an acquittal or retry a defendant on an acquitted count.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Georgia argues this case is a poor procedural vehicle because McElrath failed to timely challenge (on rehearing of his first appeal) the Georgia Supreme Court’s sua sponte decision in McElrath I to vacate both the conviction and the acquittal; law-of-the-case doctrine then barred him from attacking that vacatur later. On the merits, Georgia contends repugnant verdicts differ from ordinary inconsistent verdicts: they reflect a legally impossible combination demonstrating jury error such that the acquittal is not a valid final judgment and may be treated as void, permitting retrial. The State also emphasizes the issue is rare and Georgia’s approach is consistent with this Court’s inconsistent-verdict and double-jeopardy precedents.
key_precedents: McElrath v. State ("McElrath I"), 308 Ga. 104 (2020) (Georgia Supreme Court vacated both conviction and acquittal as repugnant/void)
McElrath v. State ("McElrath II"), 315 Ga. 126 (2022) (law-of-the-case barred renewed attack on vacatur; retrial allowed)
Turner v. State, 283 Ga. 17 (2008) (Georgia repugnant-verdicts doctrine; historically vacating conviction while leaving acquittal intact)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best contention—that Georgia may treat a “repugnant” verdict as void and therefore akin to a mistrial—fails because it elevates a state-law label over the Double Jeopardy Clause’s functional rule: a jury’s not-guilty verdict returned in open court terminates jeopardy on that offense. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Evans v. Michigan is decisive for a minimalist disposition: we look to the substance of the factfinder’s resolution of guilt, and even an erroneous acquittal is final and unreviewable if the remedy would be retrial. Justice Kagan’s citation to Martin Linen and the inconsistent-verdict line (Powell/Dunn) further narrows the ground—this case is not about regulating state verdict-management generally, but about the constitutional non-nullifiability of an acquittal once entered. The State remains free to adopt prospective procedures (polling, clarification before discharge) to avoid repugnancy, but it cannot vacate an acquittal after the fact to permit a second prosecution for the same offense.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest conceivable respondent argument is that Georgia may treat a “repugnant” acquittal as a nullity akin to a mistrial, but that characterization cannot alter the Double Jeopardy Clause’s original meaning: once a jury returns a not-guilty verdict, jeopardy terminates and the government may not try again for the same offence. Chief Justice Roberts correctly emphasizes that Georgia’s label cannot convert an acquittal into something reviewable without undermining the Clause’s core protection, a point consistent with the Founding-era understanding of jury acquittals as final. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Evans reinforces the functional inquiry: the Constitution looks to whether the factfinder resolved guilt, not to a State’s post hoc “void” label. No colleague has identified any historical practice or precedent allowing the State to vacate an acquittal to enable retrial, so my position remains unchanged.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention remains that Georgia may deem a “repugnant” acquittal void, akin to a mistrial, so jeopardy never terminated—but as Chief Justice Roberts notes, the federal Double Jeopardy inquiry turns on the functional reality that the jury returned a not-guilty verdict in open court. Justice Barrett’s reliance on Evans v. Michigan is particularly telling for a textualist approach: an acquittal is defined by its substance—resolution of guilt in the defendant’s favor—not by a State’s post hoc label, even if the result is legally mistaken or irrational. Justice Kagan is also right that Dunn/Powell and Bravo-Fernandez foreclose carving out an inconsistency-based exception, because that would invite States to reclassify disfavored acquittals and erode the Clause’s bright-line finality rule recognized in Fong Foo and Martin Linen. Practical law-enforcement concerns cannot justify a rule that permits retrial after an acquittal on the same offense, though States remain free to adopt prospective verdict-management procedures before discharge.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best contention—that Georgia can treat a “repugnant verdict” as a nullity akin to a mistrial—fails once we confront the constitutional substance: an unambiguous not-guilty verdict was returned in open court, and our Double Jeopardy cases make that acquittal final even if irrational. Justice Kagan’s point that Powell/Dunn reject inconsistency as a basis to upset an acquittal is decisive for me because Georgia’s doctrine is, functionally, an inconsistency-based exception dressed up as “voidness.” Justice Barrett’s reliance on Evans strengthens the analysis under my pragmatic lens: state-law labeling cannot be allowed to reopen exposure to conviction, because that invites retrials that fall hardest on defendants least able to endure repeated prosecutions. I agree with the Chief Justice that a narrow rule—acquittal finality bars retrial—still leaves States room to manage verdict clarification prospectively without nullifying acquittals after the fact.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Respondent’s best point remains the “void/repugnant verdict” characterization—treating the acquittal as a nullity akin to a mistrial—but Evans requires a functional inquiry, and functionally the jury resolved guilt on that count in the defendant’s favor. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis that jeopardy terminates upon a not-guilty verdict returned in open court aligns with Martin Linen and Fong Foo’s bright line: even an erroneous acquittal is final when the alternative is renewed exposure to conviction. Justice Barrett’s workability concern is decisive for me as a pragmatic textualist: a state-law repugnancy exception would invite after-the-fact reclassification of acquittals and erode the administrable rule our inconsistent-verdict cases (Dunn/Powell/Bravo-Fernandez) presuppose. Nothing cited by colleagues suggests any historically or doctrinally recognized category of “non-acquittal acquittals” that would allow retrial for the same offense.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point is that Georgia’s “repugnant verdict” rule treats the not-guilty finding as a legal nullity—more like a mistrial or nonverdict—so (the State says) jeopardy never terminated. But that characterization cannot control the Fifth Amendment’s meaning: as Justice Thomas notes, the original understanding and our cases (Fong Foo; Evans) treat an acquittal—however irrational or legally mistaken—as the event that ends jeopardy and bars a second bite at the apple. Justice Kagan’s emphasis on Martin Linen and Scott reinforces the functional inquiry: this was a jury resolution of criminal liability on that count, so the State may not “otherwise upset” it by relabeling it “void.” Allowing States to nullify acquittals whenever verdicts are “repugnant” would invite precisely the sort of post hoc reclassification that would hollow out the Double Jeopardy Clause’s bright-line protection.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that Georgia can deem a “repugnant” acquittal void and thus like a mistrial—fails because, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Double Jeopardy turns on the functional constitutional reality that a jury returned a not-guilty verdict in open court resolving guilt on that count. Evans v. Michigan, highlighted by Justice Barrett, is especially on point for my methodology: we look to substance over state-law labels, and even a legally erroneous acquittal is final when the remedy would be renewed exposure to conviction. Justice Thomas’s historical account further undercuts any state-law “nullity” exception by showing no traditional practice of governmental nullification of acquittals once rendered. Institutionally, a bright-line rule—acquittal terminates jeopardy—avoids inviting States to relabel disfavored acquittals case-by-case and better preserves the Court’s legitimacy and administrability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent-side contention would be that Georgia may deem a “repugnant” not-guilty verdict void—akin to no verdict or a mistrial—so jeopardy never terminated and retrial is permissible. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, our cases treat an acquittal’s constitutional character as a matter of substance, not state-law labels: under Fong Foo and Evans, an acquittal is final “even if … egregiously erroneous,” and cannot be set aside as a predicate for a second prosecution for the same offense. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Powell and Bravo-Fernandez further reinforces that inconsistency between counts is not a constitutionally permissible ground to nullify an acquittal; it is precisely the kind of post hoc rationalization that would invite States to reclassify acquittals whenever inconvenient. On an original public meaning and precedent-based approach, the bright-line rule is decisive: once the jury returns not guilty on the offense, jeopardy terminates and the State may not retry that offense.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest possible respondent argument is that Georgia’s “repugnant verdict” rule treats the verdicts as legally impossible and therefore a nullity akin to a mistrial, but that framing cannot survive our functional Double Jeopardy doctrine: once a jury returns a not-guilty verdict, jeopardy terminates and the State cannot relabel that acquittal into something reviewable. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Martin Linen and Powell reinforces that federal law looks to the substance of an acquittal and has long tolerated inconsistent verdicts without permitting the government to upset the acquittal. Justice Thomas’s historical point further confirms that an acquittal’s finality was the baseline rule, and Evans v. Michigan makes clear that even serious legal error does not authorize retrial after an acquittal. On a pragmatic, procedure-focused view, allowing a “repugnant” exception would invite states to circumvent the Clause through nomenclature, undermining fair notice and the jury’s constitutional role.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause bars a second prosecution once a jury has returned an acquittal, and this Court has treated that bar as absolute even when the acquittal is mistaken or legally flawed. Under Fong Foo v. United States and United States v. Martin Linen Supply Co., an acquittal is final and not reviewable in a manner that would expose the defendant to retrial; likewise, inconsistent-verdict doctrine (Dunn v. United States; Bravo-Fernandez v. United States) does not permit the State to nullify the acquittal while retrying the same offense. Georgia’s “repugnant verdict” label cannot convert a jury’s not-guilty verdict into a nullity akin to a mistrial without undermining the Clause’s core protection and this Court’s settled precedent. Whatever the procedural objections under state law (law-of-the-case), the narrow federal constitutional rule is that an acquittal—once returned—precludes retrial for the same offense under the Fifth Amendment as incorporated against the States.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Fifth Amendment provides that no person shall “be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb,” and at the Founding an acquittal by a jury ended jeopardy and was not subject to governmental nullification or appellate review. This Court’s precedents reflect that original understanding: even an “egregiously erroneous” acquittal is final and bars retrial, whether entered by judge or jury. See Fong Foo v. United States, 369 U.S. 141, 143 (1962); Evans v. Michigan, 568 U.S. 313, 318 (2013). Georgia’s labeling an acquittal “repugnant” and treating it as void is functionally a post-acquittal set-aside that exposes the defendant to a second prosecution for the same offense, which the Double Jeopardy Clause forbids.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause’s text bars putting a person “twice in jeopardy” for the same offense, and this Court has treated a jury’s not-guilty verdict as final for that purpose even when it is plainly mistaken or inconsistent with other verdicts. Under Fong Foo v. United States and Evans v. Michigan, an acquittal—however “egregiously erroneous”—cannot be reviewed or set aside as a predicate for retrial, and Bravo-Fernandez confirms that even inconsistent verdict pairs leave “the acquittals themselves” inviolate. Georgia’s characterization of the acquittal as “repugnant” or “void” is a label that cannot override the constitutional finality of an acquittal once the jury has returned it in open court. Whatever the practical frustrations for law enforcement, allowing the State to vacate an acquittal and retry would create an exception that this Court’s double-jeopardy precedents foreclose.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause forbids a second prosecution after an acquittal, and that protection applies even when the acquittal is legally mistaken or inconsistent with another verdict. This Court has held that an acquittal is “absolutely final” and cannot be reviewed or set aside without placing the defendant twice in jeopardy, even if it rests on an “egregiously erroneous foundation.” Fong Foo v. United States, 369 U.S. 141, 143 (1962); see also Evans v. Michigan, 568 U.S. 313, 318 (2013); Bravo-Fernandez v. United States, 580 U.S. 5, 24 (2016) (acquittals in inconsistent-verdict cases “remain inviolate”). Georgia’s “repugnant verdict” label cannot convert a jury’s not-guilty verdict into a nullity and authorize retrial for the same offense consistent with the Fifth Amendment as incorporated against the States.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause bars a second trial once there has been an acquittal—i.e., a jury resolution, correct or not, of the defendant’s criminal liability on that count—and the State may not “appeal or otherwise upset[] such an acquittal.” United States v. Martin Linen Supply Co., 430 U.S. 564, 571 (1977); United States v. Scott, 437 U.S. 82, 96 (1978). Georgia’s “repugnant verdict” label does not change the constitutional character of the jury’s not-guilty verdict: under United States v. Powell, 469 U.S. 57, 65 (1984), inconsistency between counts is not a basis for setting aside an acquittal, and treating it as “void” would create an unworkable exception that allows retrial precisely where the Constitution’s protection is at its apex. Whatever state-law authority Georgia has to manage inconsistent verdicts, the Fifth Amendment (as incorporated through the Fourteenth) does not permit vacating an acquittal to enable retrial for the same offense.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Fifth Amendment’s Double Jeopardy Clause, as originally understood and as this Court has long held, forbids a second prosecution after an acquittal, because the jury’s not-guilty verdict terminates jeopardy for that offense. Under Fong Foo v. United States, 369 U.S. 141, 143 (1962), an acquittal is “final” and cannot be set aside “without putting [the defendant] twice in jeopardy,” even if the verdict rests on an “egregiously erroneous foundation,” a rule reaffirmed in Evans v. Michigan and consistent with Dunn and Powell’s acceptance that inconsistent verdicts may stand. Georgia’s characterization of an acquittal as “repugnant” or “void” cannot overcome the Constitution’s bright-line protection: once the jury has acquitted, the State may not nullify that verdict and retry the defendant for the same offense. Separation-of-powers and the rule-of-law values embedded in the Double Jeopardy Clause require respecting the jury’s dispositive judgment, even when it produces an anomalous pairing with a conviction on another count.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause bars retrial after an acquittal, and this Court has repeatedly treated an acquittal as final even when it rests on legal error, jury mistake, or irrationality. Under Fong Foo v. United States and Evans v. Michigan, an acquittal cannot be vacated to permit a second prosecution for the same offense, and inconsistent verdict doctrine (Dunn; Powell; Bravo-Fernandez) likewise preserves the acquittal’s finality despite inconsistency with a conviction. Georgia’s “repugnant verdict” label cannot convert a jury’s not-guilty verdict into a nullity without undermining that settled rule and inviting case-by-case recharacterization of acquittals. Practical workability and institutional legitimacy also favor a bright-line rule: when a jury returns an acquittal, jeopardy terminates on that count and the State may not retry it.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause’s text—“nor shall any person be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb”—is best read to bar a second trial once a jury has returned a not-guilty verdict on that offense, because the defendant has already been placed in jeopardy and then acquitted. This Court has repeatedly held that an acquittal is “final” and “could not be reviewed … without putting [the defendant] twice in jeopardy,” even if the acquittal rests on an “egregiously erroneous foundation,” see Fong Foo v. United States, 369 U.S. 141, 143 (1962), and Evans v. Michigan confirms that the Constitution looks to the functional substance of an acquittal rather than state-law characterization. Georgia’s “repugnant/void” label cannot constitutionally nullify the jury’s acquittal so as to permit retrial for the same offense, because that would allow the State a second opportunity to convict after an acquittal, which the Clause forbids. Whatever the procedural posture in state court, the federal constitutional rule is categorical: an acquittal terminates jeopardy and precludes retrial on that count.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Fifth Amendment’s Double Jeopardy Clause, incorporated against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment, treats a jury’s not-guilty verdict as final and terminative of jeopardy, even if it is legally or factually mistaken. This Court has repeatedly held that an acquittal cannot be vacated or used as the basis for a second trial—"even though the acquittal may appear to be erroneous"—including where the acquittal is inconsistent with another verdict returned in the same case. See Fong Foo v. United States, 369 U.S. 141, 143 (1962); Bravo-Fernandez v. United States, 580 U.S. 5, 11 (2016); Sanabria v. United States, 437 U.S. 54, 64 (1978). Georgia’s “repugnant verdict” label cannot convert an acquittal into a nullity akin to a mistrial without undermining the jury’s constitutional role and exposing the defendant to the precise harm the Clause forbids: a second prosecution for the same offense after acquittal.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Double Jeopardy Clause permits Georgia to vacate a jury’s not-guilty verdict as “repugnant” (and therefore “void”) and retry the defendant on that same count after an appeal.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution, Fifth Amendment Double Jeopardy Clause (as incorporated against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: McElrath argues that a jury’s acquittal is final for double-jeopardy purposes even if it is logically irreconcilable with a conviction on another count; labeling the acquittal “repugnant” or “void” cannot eliminate constitutional finality, so Georgia’s vacatur of his acquittal and subsequent retrial on malice murder violates the Double Jeopardy Clause. He further contends that “repugnant” verdicts are effectively just a subset of inconsistent verdicts, which under U.S. Supreme Court precedent do not allow the State to set aside an acquittal to get a second chance to convict.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Georgia argues that the case is a poor vehicle because McElrath failed to timely challenge (on rehearing of his first appeal) the Georgia Supreme Court’s sua sponte decision vacating both the conviction and the acquittal; under state procedural doctrines like law-of-the-case, he is now barred from attacking that vacatur, making his double-jeopardy theory derivative and procedurally complicated. On the merits, Georgia contends there is a meaningful difference between ordinary inconsistent verdicts (tolerated because they may reflect leniency or compromise) and “repugnant” verdicts (which Georgia characterizes as legally impossible verdicts showing error and therefore void), and that treating a void acquittal as non-final for purposes of retrial does not conflict with this Court’s double-jeopardy and inconsistent-verdict precedents. Georgia also asserts the issue is unlikely to recur and that Georgia’s past practice suggests the state court may not repeat vacating acquittals in future repugnancy cases.

John Roberts.reasoning: The State’s strongest point—that Georgia may deem a “repugnant” acquittal void ab initio and thus avoid a second jeopardy—fails because our Double Jeopardy cases turn on the substance of what the jury did, not a post hoc state-law label. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Ball is particularly compelling: an acquittal is not subject to “review on error or otherwise,” which forecloses a doctrinal maneuver that effectively authorizes appellate nullification of a not-guilty verdict. As Justice Thomas and Justice Alito emphasize, Evans and Fong Foo make the rule categorical even for “egregiously erroneous” acquittals, and the inconsistent-verdict line (Dunn/Powell/Bravo-Fernandez) treats the acquittal as inviolate while permitting only the conviction to be disturbed. A narrow, legitimacy-protecting holding is sufficient: when a jury in a court of competent jurisdiction returns a verdict of acquittal, the Double Jeopardy Clause bars vacatur and retrial on that count, regardless of inconsistency with other counts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument would be that Georgia may treat a “repugnant” not-guilty verdict as void ab initio, meaning jeopardy never terminated; but that label cannot overcome the Fifth Amendment’s original public meaning, which forbade the sovereign from undoing an acquittal and trying again. As the Chief Justice notes, our cases make the acquittal’s finality “unassailable,” and Evans v. Michigan and Fong Foo confirm that even an “egregiously erroneous” acquittal remains an acquittal for double-jeopardy purposes. Justice Kagan’s citation to Ball underscores the same point: an acquittal ends the prosecution “on error or otherwise,” so state-law characterization cannot transform substance into a nullity. Because Georgia’s vacatur authorizes retrial on the same offense after a formally returned not-guilty verdict, it squarely triggers the Double Jeopardy Clause.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The State’s best effort—recasting the jury’s not-guilty verdict as “void” or a “nullity” under Georgia’s repugnancy doctrine—fails because the Double Jeopardy Clause turns on the functional reality that the jury returned an acquittal in a court of competent jurisdiction, not on a post hoc state-law label. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Evans and Fong Foo is decisive for me: those cases make clear that even an irrational or legally erroneous acquittal is constitutionally final and cannot be vacated to authorize a second prosecution for the same offense. Justice Kagan’s Ball point reinforces the administrable bright line our precedents require—no government “review on error or otherwise” when the consequence is renewed jeopardy—and the inconsistent-verdict line (Dunn/Powell/Bravo-Fernandez) cuts against Georgia by treating the acquittal as inviolate even when logically awkward. Accepting Georgia’s approach would invite routine relitigation of acquittals whenever a court deems the verdicts incompatible, undermining the Clause’s core protection in precisely the way our substance-over-form doctrine forbids.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest opposing argument would be that a “repugnant” acquittal is void under state law and therefore never terminated jeopardy, but that framing cannot survive our functional Double Jeopardy cases: a formally returned not-guilty verdict is an acquittal for federal constitutional purposes, even if irrational or legally mistaken. Chief Justice Roberts’s point that an acquittal’s “finality is unassailable” tracks Evans and Fong Foo and forecloses any state effort to relabel an acquittal to secure a retrial. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Ball reinforces the administrable bright-line rule that the government cannot obtain “review on error or otherwise” when the result would be renewed jeopardy. Pragmatically, allowing states to void acquittals deemed inconsistent would predictably fall hardest on defendants least able to endure repeated prosecutions, undermining the jury’s protective function and access to justice.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The State’s best point remains the “repugnant verdict = legal nullity” move, but it collapses under the substance-over-label rule: what matters for Double Jeopardy is that the jury actually returned a not-guilty verdict on a count in a court of competent jurisdiction, not how Georgia later characterizes the inconsistency. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Evans and Fong Foo is decisive for me because those cases refuse to permit retrial even when the acquittal rests on serious legal error, and Ball’s “on error or otherwise” language makes the bright-line administrable. Justice Alito’s workability concern reinforces the textual/doctrinal point: an exception for “void” acquittals would invite post hoc judicial review of not-guilty verdicts and erode finality in exactly the way the Clause is meant to prevent. Nothing in Dunn/Powell/Bravo-Fernandez authorizes vacating the acquittal itself; they treat the acquittal as fixed even when the overall verdict set is logically messy.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The best argument for the State is that a “repugnant” acquittal is a legal nullity under Georgia procedure, so jeopardy never terminates; but the Double Jeopardy Clause’s protection turns on what occurred in substance—a jury returned a not-guilty verdict within a court of competent jurisdiction—not on a State’s after-the-fact label. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas both emphasize, our cases treat an acquittal as categorically final “even if … egregiously erroneous,” and that bright-line rule would be empty if States could recharacterize acquittals as “void” whenever they seem logically incompatible with a conviction. Justice Alito’s practical point reinforces the constitutional one: permitting vacatur of acquittals based on perceived inconsistency invites routine second attempts to convict, precisely what the Clause forbids. I therefore remain with petitioner because neither text, history, nor precedent supports an exception allowing retrial after a formally returned acquittal.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The State’s best point remains the “void ab initio” framing—if the acquittal is a nullity under Georgia’s repugnancy doctrine, jeopardy supposedly never terminated—but that is precisely the kind of label-driven maneuver our Double Jeopardy cases reject. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, Evans and Fong Foo turn on what happened in substance: a jury returned a formal not-guilty verdict in a court of competent jurisdiction, and that ends jeopardy even if the verdict is irrational or legally mistaken. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Ball strengthens the administrable, legitimacy-protecting bright line—acquittals are not reviewable “on error or otherwise”—which would be badly eroded if States could later deem acquittals “void” whenever they appear inconsistent. On an institutionalist, precedent-focused approach, the Court should hold narrowly that Georgia may address inconsistency by disturbing the conviction if state law allows, but it cannot vacate the acquittal and retry that count without violating the Double Jeopardy Clause.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent-style contention would be that Georgia’s “repugnant verdict” rule treats the not-guilty finding as a legal nullity, so there was no valid acquittal to trigger double-jeopardy finality. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, our Double Jeopardy cases look to the substance of what occurred—a formal not-guilty verdict by the trier of fact in a court of competent jurisdiction—not to a State’s post hoc label, and Fong Foo and Evans make clear that even an “egregiously erroneous” acquittal is still an acquittal for federal constitutional purposes. Justice Kagan’s citation to Ball underscores the administrable, bright-line principle that acquittals are not reviewable “on error or otherwise,” and carving an inconsistency/repugnancy exception would invite exactly the second chance to convict the Clause forbids. Georgia may set aside the conviction if state law permits, but it cannot vacate the acquittal and retry that count without placing the defendant twice in jeopardy for the same offense.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The State’s best move—relabeling a “repugnant” acquittal as void ab initio—still fails because Double Jeopardy turns on the substance of the jury’s resolution of guilt, not a post hoc state-law characterization. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Sotomayor stress, Evans and Fong Foo make acquittal finality categorical even when the verdict is irrational or legally wrong, and Georgia’s doctrine cannot create an “egregiousness” exception without inviting routine judicial undoing of not-guilty verdicts. Justice Kagan’s invocation of Ball strengthens the administrability point: an acquittal is not reviewable “on error or otherwise,” so vacatur-and-retrial is precisely what the Clause forbids. Pragmatically and procedurally, allowing states to nullify acquittals based on inconsistency would undermine the jury’s protective role and expose defendants—especially those least able to bear repeated prosecutions—to renewed jeopardy.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause forbids a State from setting aside a jury’s acquittal and retrying the defendant on that same count, even if the acquittal is legally or logically mistaken. Our cases make clear that an acquittal’s “finality is unassailable,” and retrial following an acquittal is barred “even if the acquittal is based upon an egregiously erroneous foundation.” Evans v. Michigan, 568 U.S. 313, 318 (2013) (quoting Fong Foo v. United States, 369 U.S. 141, 143 (1962)); see also Bravo-Fernandez v. United States, 580 U.S. 5, 24 (2016) (inconsistent verdicts do not permit the government to challenge the acquittal). Whatever Georgia may do with a repugnancy doctrine as to convictions, labeling an acquittal “repugnant” or “void” cannot circumvent the Fifth Amendment’s bar on a second prosecution for the same offense.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Fifth Amendment provides that no person shall “be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb,” and at the Founding that protection forbade the sovereign from undoing a jury’s acquittal and trying again. This Court’s cases reflect that original meaning: a formally returned acquittal is final for double-jeopardy purposes even if it rests on legal error or is inconsistent with another verdict. Under Fong Foo v. United States and Evans v. Michigan, a mistaken or “egregiously erroneous” acquittal remains an acquittal, and permitting Georgia to label it “repugnant” or “void” would allow precisely the second bite at the apple the Clause prohibits. Because Georgia’s vacatur functionally nullifies an acquittal and authorizes retrial on the same count, it violates the Double Jeopardy Clause as incorporated against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause’s text—protecting against being “twice put in jeopardy of life or limb”—has long been applied to make an acquittal final, even when legally wrong, because any state effort to set it aside necessarily subjects the defendant to a second jeopardy on the same offense. Under Fong Foo v. United States and its successors, including United States v. Martin Linen Supply Co. and Evans v. Michigan, an acquittal “terminates the prosecution” for that count and is not reviewable in a way that would allow retrial, even if the acquittal rests on an “egregiously erroneous foundation.” Georgia’s relabeling of the jury’s not-guilty verdict as “repugnant” or “void” cannot circumvent that constitutional finality; this Court’s inconsistent-verdict cases likewise treat acquittals as “inviolate” notwithstanding logical tension with other counts (see Bravo-Fernandez v. United States; Dunn v. United States; United States v. Powell). Practical consequences reinforce that conclusion: permitting States to nullify acquittals deemed inconsistent would invite routine post hoc attacks on jury not-guilty verdicts and materially erode the finality the Clause was designed to secure.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause, as incorporated through the Fourteenth Amendment, bars a State from retrying a defendant on a count for which the jury returned a not-guilty verdict, even if that acquittal is logically inconsistent with a conviction on another count. This Court has repeatedly held that an acquittal “terminate[s] the initial jeopardy” and is “final” even when “based upon an egregiously erroneous foundation,” foreclosing any state effort to relabel it as “repugnant” or “void” to obtain a second chance to convict. See Fong Foo v. United States and Evans v. Michigan; inconsistent-verdict doctrine may justify disturbing a conviction, but it cannot authorize setting aside an acquittal and subjecting the defendant—especially one facing life-and-death penal consequences—to renewed exposure and the anxiety and imbalance of power that retrial entails. Georgia’s asserted procedural objections cannot override the federal constitutional finality of a jury acquittal where the trial court had jurisdiction and the verdict was actually returned.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause provides that no person shall “be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb,” and this Court has treated a jury’s acquittal as terminating jeopardy in a way that is not reviewable “on error or otherwise.” Ball v. United States, 163 U.S. 662, 671 (1896). That rule applies even when an acquittal rests on a legally mistaken or irrational basis: in Fong Foo v. United States, 369 U.S. 141, 143 (1962), we held an acquittal may not be vacated despite an “egregiously erroneous foundation.” Georgia’s “repugnant” label cannot convert what is functionally an acquittal into a nullity without undermining the Clause’s administrable, bright-line finality rule and inviting retrials whenever a court later deems a not-guilty verdict “impossible.”

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause provides that no person shall “be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy,” and at the founding an acquittal—right or wrong—ended the prosecution on that charge. This Court’s precedents treat a not-guilty verdict as final and unreviewable even if “egregiously erroneous,” because any attempt to set it aside and retry the defendant would place him twice in jeopardy. See Fong Foo v. United States, 369 U.S. 141, 143 (1962), reaffirmed in Evans v. Michigan, 568 U.S. 313, 318 (2013); and in the inconsistent-verdict context, the acquittal “remain[s] inviolate,” Bravo-Fernandez v. United States, 580 U.S. 5, 24 (2016). Georgia may label an acquittal “repugnant” or “void” as a matter of state law, but state-law characterization cannot erase the federal constitutional finality of an acquittal for double-jeopardy purposes.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause bars retrial after an acquittal, and this Court has repeatedly held that an acquittal is final even if legally erroneous or irrational. See Fong Foo v. United States, 369 U.S. 141, 143 (1962), and Evans v. Michigan, 568 U.S. 313, 318 (2013) (reaffirming that retrial is barred even when the acquittal rests on an “egregiously erroneous foundation”). Georgia’s characterization of the not-guilty verdict as “repugnant” or “void” cannot override the constitutional finality of a jury acquittal, and our inconsistent-verdict cases (e.g., Dunn and Powell, as applied in Bravo-Fernandez) likewise treat the acquittal as “inviolate” notwithstanding logical inconsistency. Practical workability and judicial restraint cut in the same direction: allowing states to relabel acquittals as void would invite ad hoc exceptions that erode a clear, administrable double-jeopardy rule.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause provides that no person shall “be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy,” and at the Founding an acquittal by the trier of fact ended the prosecution and barred a second trial on the same charge. This Court’s precedents treat an acquittal as final for double-jeopardy purposes even if legally erroneous or logically inconsistent with another count: a “mistaken acquittal is an acquittal nonetheless,” Evans v. Michigan, 568 U.S. 313, 318 (2013) (citing Fong Foo v. United States, 369 U.S. 141 (1962)), and the State may not set it aside to obtain another opportunity to convict. That logic applies with equal force where Georgia labels the acquittal “repugnant” or “void,” because the constitutional bar turns on the substance—an acquittal on guilt or innocence—not the State’s characterization. While Georgia may vacate a conviction infected by inconsistency, it cannot vacate the acquittal itself and retry the defendant on that same count without violating the Double Jeopardy Clause.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause, as incorporated against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment, bars a second prosecution after an acquittal, and this Court has treated that finality as categorical even when the acquittal rests on legal error. Under Fong Foo v. United States and Evans v. Michigan, an acquittal—however “egregiously erroneous”—terminates jeopardy and is not subject to state relabeling as “void” to permit retrial. Georgia’s “repugnant verdict” doctrine functions like inconsistent-verdict scenarios addressed in Dunn, Powell, and Bravo-Fernandez, where the conviction may fall but “the acquittals themselves remain inviolate.” Whatever state procedural default arguments exist, the practical consequence of allowing vacatur-and-retrial of a not-guilty verdict would undermine the jury’s role and invite post hoc nullification of acquittals, contrary to the core procedural fairness the Double Jeopardy Clause guarantees.
